tldr: We compared 14 unsupervised environment design (UED) and reinforcement learning curriculum methods—originally developed in 2D environments—across five quadruped robots on a shared 3D rough terrain benchmark. The results show that no single method works best across all robots and terrains. In many cases, simply starting with easy terrains performs just as well or better, while the success-driven terrain curriculum (Terrain-CL) widely used in robotics practice proves exceptionally solid.
hero_caption: The five quadruped robots evaluated in this benchmark (W01-TEK, Go1, Go2, Barkour vB, and Spot) standing on the same terrain genome at difficulty 0.6. Absolute terrain dimensions and camera distances are scaled to each robot's body size (scale factor $s$), enabling a fair comparison under a unified protocol.
overview:
When training quadruped robots with deep reinforcement learning, the curriculum design—what terrains are shown and in what order—greatly influences locomotion performance. In machine learning, Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) methods like PAIRED and ACCEL, which automatically generate and curate environment parameters, have received significant attention. However, these methods have been evaluated mostly on 2D mazes or simple environments like BipedalWalker, leaving it unclear how well they transfer to 3D, high-dimensional, contact-rich quadruped robots. Meanwhile, robotics practitioners rely on hand-crafted heuristic terrain curricula as the de facto standard, yet systematic comparisons against UED methods have been lacking.

To bridge this gap, the authors built a large-scale benchmark comparing 14 curriculum learning methods (UED, domain randomisation, and robotics curricula) under a single protocol and matched environment-step budgets across five quadrupeds: the closed-chain W01-TEK and four open-chain robots (Unitree Go1, Go2, Google Barkour vB, and Boston Dynamics Spot). Across 350 training runs, the benchmark revealed that no single method is in the top group across all robots and terrains. On Go1 and Barkour, simple domain randomisation variants that merely include easy or low-difficulty levels (DR-easy and DR-mixed) entered the top group without any complex level curation. The success-driven terrain curriculum from legged-robot practice (Terrain-CL) was in a top group most often (13 out of 20 categories), followed by ACCEL (11 times), whereas uniform domain randomisation never made it into a top group.
contributions: Built a large-scale, open-source benchmark in MuJoCo MJX featuring five diverse quadruped robots (including a closed-chain design) and a shared 8-dimensional interpretable rough terrain parameter space.

Fairly evaluated 14 methods—from state-of-the-art UED algorithms (PAIRED, ACCEL, SFL) to standard robotics terrain curricula and control baselines—using the same PPO agent and matched environment-step budgets across 5 seeds (350 runs in total).

Established a multifaceted evaluation protocol (in-distribution random terrains, held-out structured terrains, capability envelopes, and level-by-level domination comparisons) and provided a per-robot guide for choosing curricula.

sections.heading: Introduction: Is It the Curriculum or Just the Easy Start?
sections.summary: While training terrain distributions dictate quadruped locomotion performance, empirical robotics heuristics and machine learning UED methods have been developed in isolation. This study builds a unified benchmark across five robots and 14 methods to test how well UED findings hold up on real-world 3D legged robots.
sections.details:
When acquiring quadruped locomotion controllers via reinforcement learning, the distribution of training terrains is critical. In robotics practice, hand-designed curricula that adjust difficulty based on traversal distance (such as the method by Rudin et al.) are widely adopted. Meanwhile, the machine learning UED (Unsupervised Environment Design) community has developed methods like PAIRED, PLR, ACCEL, and SFL, which automatically generate and score environments (levels) based on agent regret or learning progress.

However, these UED methods have mostly been compared on 2D grid worlds or simple BipedalWalker tasks. No benchmark had applied them to 3D quadruped robots with high degrees of freedom and complex contacts. Using MuJoCo MJX, this study thoroughly compares 14 curriculum methods across five quadrupeds of varying kinematics and scale (W01-TEK, Go1, Go2, Barkour vB, and Spot) using the same PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) student and matched step budgets.

The central question is: does sophisticated level generation and prioritized replay really matter, or does simply starting training on easy terrains do the trick? By assessing agents on in-distribution random levels, held-out structured terrains, and capability limits, the authors reveal how to choose the right curriculum for each robot.

sections.heading: Related Work: ML's UED Meets Robotics Terrain Curricula
sections.summary: This section traces two separate lines of research: adversarial and regret-based UED versus progress-based robotics terrain curricula. The study brings them together in a direct head-to-head comparison under a shared terrain representation and evaluation standard.
sections.details:
### Trends in UED (Unsupervised Environment Design)
In UED, a teacher proposes environment parameters to maximize the generalization performance of a student agent. PAIRED trains an environment generator to maximize regret, defined as the return difference between two student policies. PLR and its variant PLR ⟂ curate randomly generated levels into a replay buffer based on high regret, while ACCEL couples this with local level mutations, achieving strong results on 2D walkers. SFL pointed out that conventional regret estimation often just tracks success rates, proposing instead to score levels by learnability (where success rate is close to 50%).

### Locomotion Curricula in Robotics
In quadruped reinforcement learning, the grid-based terrain curriculum proposed by Rudin et al. (Terrain-CL), which advances or demotes difficulty based on walking distance, has become the de facto standard. Other efforts, such as LP-ACRL, sample terrains based on learning progress (return delta). However, these have only been evaluated on individual robots with custom baselines, and no study had compared robots of differing sizes and kinematic chains on equal footing.

sections.heading: Benchmark Setup: Five Robots and 14 Curricula
sections.summary: An 8-dimensional interpretable terrain parameter space was designed for five robots, including the closed-chain W01-TEK. Using the same PPO student, 14 methods—spanning UED, domain randomisation, and robotics curricula—are evaluated under matched environment-step budgets.
sections.details:
### Robot and Task Setup
The benchmark features five quadrupeds: the closed-chain W01-TEK (with passive 4-bar linkages developed at Wrocław University of Science and Technology) and four open-chain robots from MuJoCo Playground and Menagerie (Unitree Go1, Go2, Google Barkour vB, and Boston Dynamics Spot). All robots learn a joystick velocity-tracking task. Actors operate blind without exteroception, while critics receive a 5×5 height scan under the torso. Fall criteria are standardized across all robots: torso height falling below 0.6× standing height or orientation tilt exceeding a set threshold.

### Terrain Representation (Level Space) and Tiled Arena
A single terrain level is defined by an 8-dimensional vector $\theta \in [0, 1]^8$ and a random seed. The eight parameters linearly map to radial slopes (-20° to +18°), radial stairs (step height -8 to +5 cm, width 15 to 60 cm), smooth noise (amplitude 0 to 10 cm), gaps (width 0 to 6 cm), and blocks (height 0 to 6 cm). Difficulty $d \in [0, 1]$ interpolates from flat terrain, with $d=0.1$ being very easy. For high throughput, a shared height field with 16×16 tiles allows parallel training across 256 distinct terrains without model recompilation.

### 14 Curriculum Methods
The benchmark evaluates a broad selection of approaches:
- **DR baselines**: Standard DR (uniform random levels), DR-easy (fixed at $d=0.1$), and DR-mixed (random difficulty $d \sim \mathcal{U}(0,1)$ per level).
- **Robotics curriculum**: Terrain-CL, adapting Rudin et al.'s progress grid to parallel lanes.
- **Replay buffer UED**: PLR ⟂ (filtering by positive return advantage) and SFL (scoring by learnability $p(1-p)$).
- **ACCEL family**: ACCEL (mutating buffer levels), ACCEL-grow (expanding difficulty bounds on mutation), ACCEL-SFL (SFL score), and ACCEL-LP (learning progress score).
- **PAIRED family**: Standard PAIRED (adversarial generator), UniBC and BiBC (stabilized with behavioral cloning), and PAIRED+Evo (replacing the generator with evolutionary mutation).

To ensure fairness, all methods receive matched environment-step budgets: 300 million steps for W01-TEK and 1 billion steps for the other robots.

captions.F3: Terrain level variations illustrated on W01-TEK. Shown from the initial flat terrain to rough terrain, uphill/downhill slopes, stairs, gaps, and blocks with individual features maximized, followed by compound random terrains at difficulty 0.5 and 1.0. The robot spawn area is always a flat disc.

sections.heading: Evaluation Protocol: Robust Metrics to Prevent Overestimation
sections.summary: Trained deterministic policies are evaluated across in-distribution random terrains, a held-out structured suite, flat ground, and capability envelopes. Cross-fitted CVaR and level-by-level domination comparisons are introduced to remove ranking noise bias.
sections.details:
### Diverse Test Sets and Headline Difficulty
Policies are evaluated deterministically without domain randomisation. Test environments include:
- **Random (in-distribution)**: 2048 genomes at difficulty $d=0.25$, $d=0.5$, and full difficulty $d=1.0$.
- **Held-out suite**: 7 feature tracks (stairs up/down, slopes, gaps, waves, blocks) across 4 intensities (28 cells × 64 instances = 1792 levels).
- **Flat**: Verifying basic walking gait stability.
- **Capability envelopes**: Incrementally increasing single features to find the 50% success boundary.

Because full difficulty ($d=1.0$) is too harsh for open-chain robots (Go1 reaches at most 19%, others below 5%), it fails to separate methods. Thus, the authors adopt $d=0.25$ as the primary headline difficulty.

### Statistical Rigor and Domination Comparisons
To evaluate robustness on the hardest 25% of levels without selection bias, cross-fitted CVaR 25 splits evaluations across two independent passes, alternating ranking and score measurement. In addition, because overall mean success can obscure where methods actually win, a level-by-level domination comparison evaluates pairwise win rates against a binomial noise reference. Methods not significantly below the best performer according to Welch's $t$-test ($p \ge 0.05$) within each robot form the 'top group'.

sections.heading: Results: No Silver Bullet, and an Easy Start Goes a Long Way
sections.summary: Detailed analysis across six questions reveals key findings: methods starting with easy levels dominate in-distribution tests, leaders often swap on held-out terrains, and all 14 methods finish within 3.8 points of each other on Spot.
sections.details:
### Q1: Who Solves In-Distribution Random Terrains?
At difficulty $d=0.25$, ACCEL-grow (91.2% success), ACCEL, and DR-mixed formed the top group on W01-TEK. On Go1, ACCEL-LP (64.0%), Terrain-CL, DR-easy, and DR-mixed led, leaving standard DR (34.9%) and PAIRED variants (24.6–33.3%) far behind. Terrain-CL, DR-easy, and ACCEL variants also led on Go2 and Barkour. On Spot, however, all 14 methods clustered within a narrow 3.8-point window (14.1% to 17.9%). Crucially, every top-group method on Go1 and Barkour—and most on W01-TEK—features easy or low-difficulty levels during training. Methods training uniformly on hard levels from the start (DR, PLR ⟂, SFL) fell behind across the board.

### Q2: Who Transfers to Held-Out Structured Terrains?
On held-out structured terrains, rankings shifted. On Go1, Terrain-CL (45.8%), ACCEL, and SFL led, while in-distribution leader ACCEL-LP dropped out. ACCEL led on Go2 (33.4%), and SFL led on Barkour (45.2%). On three robots (Go1, Go2, and Barkour), the in-distribution leader was not the held-out leader. Furthermore, while DR-easy and Terrain-CL tied on random terrains, Terrain-CL outperformed DR-easy by 7.2 points on held-out terrains (45.8% vs 38.6% on Go1).

### Q3–Q6: Hard Terrains, Limits, Compute, and Reproducibility
Only W01-TEK (up to 43.5%) and Go1 (up to 19.1%) achieved meaningful success at full difficulty ($d=1.0$), with Terrain-CL leading both. Standard DR failed to make the top group even on the full difficulty it was trained on. In capability envelopes (Q4), stair-climbing step height separated curricula, while no method enabled Go2 or Spot to cross gaps. Regarding compute cost (Q5), PAIRED variants took roughly 2× the GPU time due to adversary rollouts, whereas all other methods took 0.5–0.9 hours per run on an H100 GPU. For reproducibility (Q6), Go2 exhibited high variance (standard deviation up to 12.7 points) due to failed training runs on some seeds, whereas DR-mixed remained remarkably consistent across all robots (standard deviation under 2.8 points).

captions.F6: Level-by-level domination comparison between ACCEL and standard DR at difficulty $d=0.25$. Cell colors show the frequency of joint success-rate pairs on a log scale; points below the diagonal indicate levels where ACCEL achieved higher success. ACCEL dominates DR on 96% of levels on Go1 and 100% on Barkour.
captions.F7: Pairwise domination matrix across all 14 methods at difficulty $d=0.25$. Cells display the proportion of levels where the row method outperforms the column method, with darker shades indicating stronger dominance. Robotics-standard Terrain-CL and mutation-based ACCEL variants clearly dominate baselines like DR and PAIRED across large regions.

sections.heading: Practical Guide: Which Curriculum Should You Actually Use?
sections.summary: Analyzing results across all robots and evaluation sets reveals the strengths and weaknesses of each method family. When in doubt, practical Terrain-CL is the top recommendation, followed by ACCEL, while simple DR-mixed or DR-easy remains surprisingly strong.
sections.details:
Based on top-group placements across all 20 evaluation categories (5 robots × 4 test sets), the authors provide practical recommendations:

- **Randomisation baselines (DR, DR-easy, DR-mixed)**:
  Standard uniform DR never entered a top group (0 out of 20) and should be avoided. However, altering the sampling distribution changes everything. DR-easy and DR-mixed require no replay buffer or score computation and share the low cost of DR, yet they reach top groups on random terrains for Go1, Barkour, and W01-TEK.

- **Robotics curriculum (Terrain-CL)**:
  Entered the top group in 13 out of 20 categories—the highest among all methods. It reached the top group in all 4 sets on Go1 and Barkour, and 3 sets on Go2. Requiring only task success and progress thresholds, it is simple, buffer-free, and remarkably robust.

- **Replay buffer methods (PLR ⟂, SFL)**:
  PLR ⟂ never reached a top group. In contrast, SFL, which scores levels by learnability, made the top group on held-out terrains for Go1, Go2, and Barkour, taking sole first place on Barkour.

- **ACCEL family**:
  Particularly strong on held-out terrains, ACCEL variants entered top groups in 11 categories, trailing only Terrain-CL. ACCEL-grow dominated on W01-TEK, while ACCEL-LP led Go1 on random terrains.

- **PAIRED family**:
  Generator-based PAIRED variants lagged behind even PLR ⟂ on four robots (excluding Spot), delivering poor performance despite costing twice the GPU compute.

**Takeaway**: If you cannot afford to benchmark multiple curricula on a new robot, your primary choice should be **Terrain-CL**, with **ACCEL** as a strong secondary option. Furthermore, always evaluate on held-out structured terrains alongside in-distribution random levels, as evaluating on random levels alone can pick the wrong method.

sections.heading: Discussion and Limitations: Did 2D Lessons Hold Up in 3D Locomotion?
sections.summary: This section examines why UED findings from 2D environments broke down in 3D quadruped locomotion, while also noting limitations around fixed step budgets and hardware-induced capacity ceilings.
sections.details:
### Discrepancies with 2D UED Assumptions
In 2D grid worlds and BipedalWalker studies (such as JaxUED and SFL), standard domain randomisation (DR) was reported as a very strong baseline. In 3D quadruped locomotion, however, uniform DR collapsed near the bottom across all robots. Thrown into harsh 3D terrains from step zero, robots fail to discover stable gaits and fall immediately, making an 'easy start' essential. Similarly, PAIRED struggled in 3D just as it did in 2D, and behavioral cloning stabilization failed to rescue it outside of Spot.

### Limitations
- **Fixed training budget**: The benchmark evaluates policies under fixed environment steps (300M for W01-TEK, 1B for others). Because learning curves for Go1 and Barkour were still trending upward at 1 billion steps, rankings could shift with longer training.
- **Hardware capacity ceilings**: Physical hardware constraints, such as joint limits and power-to-weight ratios, cap the maximum level difficulty each robot can solve. Consequently, scores cannot be pooled across robots, keeping comparisons within each platform.
- **Curriculum implementations**: Terrain-CL and ACCEL-LP adapt original designs (such as legged_gym's fixed terrain types or LP-ACRL's discrete task sets) to fit this benchmark's 8D continuous level space and parallel lane architecture.

sections.heading: Appendix: Training Details, Terrain Progressions, and Compute Footprint
sections.summary: Details on robot size normalization, fall criteria, how terrain parameters evolved during training for each curriculum, and how the simulation environment achieved fast turnaround times of around an hour per run.
sections.details:
### Robot Scaling and Normalization
To account for physical differences, each robot is assigned a scale factor $s$ based on standing torso height (W01-TEK: 0.5, Go1: 0.4, Go2: 0.4, Barkour: 0.4, Spot: 0.7). Terrain heights, widths, and target travel distances ($s$ meters) are scaled by $s$. Because Spot has a lower top speed relative to its size, its episode length is extended to 780 steps (15.6 s) compared to 300 steps (6.0 s) for the other robots to allow equal target traversal.

### Evolution of Training Terrains
As shown in Figure 10, the physical parameters presented to the student agent during training differ drastically across curricula. Standard DR samples harsh parameters throughout training. In contrast, Terrain-CL and ACCEL variants begin near flat terrain and smoothly ramp up stair heights, slope angles, and noise amplitude as the agent improves. For robots prone to early falls like Go2 and Barkour, this gradual ramp-up is critical to learning.

### Compute and Implementation
Leveraging MuJoCo MJX (Warp backend for W01-TEK, JAX backend for the others), 1 billion RL steps train in just 0.9 to 1.1 hours on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU. The entire benchmark of 350 runs required only 306 GPU hours, making this unprecedented comparison across 14 methods, 5 robots, and 5 seeds computationally tractable.

captions.F10: Evolution of physical parameter averages and genome distance from flat ground presented to the student agent across training steps. While standard DR (blue) remains at high difficulty throughout, Terrain-CL (red) and ACCEL variants (pink/light green) start near zero and smoothly scale difficulty upward as training progresses.

takeaways: Before adopting complex UED algorithms, ensure your training includes an 'easy start'—simply beginning with low-difficulty levels outperforms standard uniform DR by a wide margin.

When choosing a default curriculum, the robotics standard 'Terrain-CL' is the top pick, followed by 'ACCEL'. Terrain-CL requires no replay buffer or complex scoring, yet it enters the top group more often than any other method.

Never evaluate curricula on in-distribution random levels alone; always include held-out structured terrains. In this benchmark, the top-performing method swapped between random and held-out test sets on three of the five robots.
UED findings from 2D domains (such as DR being strong or PAIRED being competitive) do not transfer directly to 3D quadruped locomotion, underscoring the need for validation on 3D physics benchmarks.
limitations: Evaluation is restricted to blind locomotion without cameras or LiDAR; performance on perceptive locomotion controllers navigating elevation changes remains untested.
All methods are evaluated at fixed step budgets (e.g., 1 billion steps), which does not rule out slower-converging methods catching up given longer training horizons.
The benchmark is conducted purely in MuJoCo MJX simulation; real-world sim-to-real transfer gaps and hardware deployment robustness were not evaluated.
